drafts.title: Keep ride comfort composed on broken pavement
drafts.description: Customers experience a composed, non‑harsh ride over broken pavement and pothole‑ridden roads — bumps feel absorbed and the car does not feel jarring to occupants.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: On a standardized broken‑pavement test course driven at 30–50 mph, no more than 20% of a representative test panel (n≥40) may rate the ride as 'harsh' or worse; objective seat‑rail vertical acceleration RMS shall not exceed 0.9 m/s² on the same course.
assumptions: Standardized broken‑pavement course and passenger panel methodology will be defined (similar to OEM ride surveys) and repeatable across vehicles.
Seat‑rail acceleration RMS threshold of 0.9 m/s² is a conservative target consistent with premium segment benchmarks.
uncertainties: Some customers' perception of 'harsh' varies with seating position and tire choice; tire/wheel options may change measured values.
Tradeoffs may be required between very low‑speed compliance and high‑speed body control.

drafts.title: Reduce distracting wind noise at highway speeds
drafts.description: When driving on the highway above 70 mph customers do not perceive wind noise as distracting; the cabin audio environment remains quiet and non‑tiring.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: At 75 mph on a level highway, measured interior A‑weighted sound pressure level attributable to wind sources at the driver's ear shall be ≤68 dB(A) and in a usability panel (n≥40) no more than 10% of participants report wind noise as 'distracting'.
assumptions: Wind‑noise attribution uses standard microphone placement at the driver's ear and spectral analysis to separate drivetrain/road from wind.
Measurement and subjective test conducted with representative trim (production glazing and mirrors).
uncertainties: Open windows, roof racks, or aftermarket accessories will change results; the acceptance applies to factory configuration.
Extreme weather (heavy crosswinds) may exceed targets intermittently.

drafts.title: Lane‑keeping assist: smooth, non‑abrupt steering in curves
drafts.description: When lane‑keeping assist is active customers experience smooth lateral guidance in curves without sudden or jarring steering inputs.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: On winding highway sections (45–75 mph) with lane‑keeping engaged, instrumented fleet testing must show: (a) maximum lateral jerk per automated intervention < 0.7 m/s³, and (b) in a driver validation panel (n≥40) ≤5% of maneuvers are rated as 'abrupt' or 'startling'.
assumptions: Tests use a representative set of curvy highway segments and production tires/steering settings.
Objective lateral jerk threshold of 0.7 m/s³ correlates with perceived abruptness in previous human factors studies.
uncertainties: Extreme lane markings, rapid cut‑ins by other vehicles, or degraded sensors may require occasional stronger interventions.
Tuning for smoothness must not unacceptably reduce lane‑centering performance in safety‑critical situations.

drafts.title: Make charging state visible at a glance via the charge port indicator
drafts.description: Customers can tell whether the vehicle is charging, paused, or fully charged without opening an app — the exterior charge‑port indicator is clearly visible and easily understood.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: The charge‑port visual indicator is legible from 3 meters at night and in daylight and is correctly interpreted by ≥90% of participants in a usability test (n≥40) across the three states: charging, paused/fault, charge complete.
assumptions: Visibility and comprehension tests include representative ambient lighting conditions (daylight, dusk, night).
Indicator will convey at least three distinct, easily distinguishable states (charging, paused/error, complete).
uncertainties: Color‑blind users require non‑color cues (blinking pattern or icon) to reach the 90% comprehension target.
Aftermarket obstructions (covers) or dirt may reduce visibility.

drafts.title: Navigation finds compatible chargers quickly and shows compatibility and availability
drafts.description: When planning or during a trip customers can quickly find chargers that are compatible with their vehicle, see connector/type, charging power, real‑time availability and payment requirements so charging stops are predictable and fast.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: For 95% of planned interstate trips between 200–800 miles, the route planner presents at least one compatible DC fast charger in each ~120‑mile segment along the route; average time for a user to identify a compatible charger and confirm compatibility ≤20 seconds in usability testing; real‑time availability and payment method information matches station status ≥95% of the time in a field validation across representative routes.
assumptions: Access to up‑to‑date third‑party charger network data (connector types, availability, payment methods) is available through partnerships or data agreements.
Compatibility logic includes vehicle charging capabilities and known adapter support.
uncertainties: Charger network data latency or API limitations may cause transient mismatches in availability.
Some rural corridors may legitimately lack compatible high‑power chargers within the segment distance.

drafts.title: Offer a clearly communicated long‑range option and disclose realistic real‑world range
drafts.description: Customers who prioritize long trips can choose a long‑range variant; real‑world expected range is clearly disclosed for typical driving conditions so buyers know whether the vehicle meets their long‑trip needs.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: A long‑range variant (or powertrain option) shall deliver a measured real‑world range of at least 400 miles under steady highway conditions (measured at 65 mph, representative ambient temperature) for ≥80% of production vehicles in a fleet test; all range claims presented in marketing and the vehicle UI shall include the test conditions used to derive the figure.
assumptions: 400‑mile real‑world BEV range is achievable in the premium segment within 3–5 years with higher‑capacity battery packs or hybrid range‑extender architectures.
Measured range uses a repeatable highway procedure (steady 65 mph, moderate ambient temperature) so customers can compare variants.
uncertainties: Some customers requested 600–700 miles; achieving those numbers without refueling (ICE or fuel‑extender) is unlikely for pure BEVs in the 3–5 year horizon and thus not set as the target.
Actual customer range will vary strongly with driving speed, temperature, load and accessory use.

drafts.title: Level 3 (conditional) type‑approval requests (customer desire)
drafts.description: Customers ask that the car receives type approval for Level 3 automated driving in specific markets (e.g. Germany).
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope for product requirements: type‑approval and homologation are regulatory processes not captured as customer‑facing functional requirements.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulatory type‑approval / homologation request — out of scope for vehicle customer‑facing functional requirements.

drafts.title: CARB emission limits compliance request (customer)
drafts.description: Customers express a desire that the powertrain complies with California (CARB) emission requirements in all US states.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope for product requirement drafts: regulatory compliance and homologation belong to certification workstreams.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulatory/homologation request — out of scope for customer‑facing requirement drafting.

drafts.title: UN R155 cybersecurity approval request (customer)
drafts.description: Customers ask that the vehicle fulfils UN R155 cybersecurity type approval.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope for product requirement drafts: certification and regulatory approvals are not written as customer‑facing functional requirements here.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulatory/certification request — handled by compliance teams, not as a customer outcome requirement.

drafts.title: Battery passport regulation compliance request (customer)
drafts.description: Customers ask that the vehicle's battery complies with the EU battery passport regulation.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope for product requirements: this is a regulatory documentation/compliance ask.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulatory compliance/documentation requirement — out of scope for customer‑facing functional requirements.

drafts.title: 800 V electrical architecture request (customer specification)
drafts.description: Customers request that the car use an 800 V electrical architecture to enable faster charging.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope (engineering specification): requests for specific electrical architectures should be handled as engineering specs or product options, not as direct customer‑facing requirements in this document.
drafts.scope_reason: Engineering specification request (voltage architecture) — out of scope. Customer outcome (faster charging) is addressed by charger/UX requirements above.

drafts.title: 22 kW onboard AC charger request (customer specification)
drafts.description: Customers request that the onboard AC charger be upgraded to 22 kW.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope (engineering specification): specifying exact charger kW belongs in engineering/option specs rather than a customer‑facing requirement; customer outcome of faster home charging can be captured via charging time/experience requirements.
drafts.scope_reason: Engineering specification request (onboard charger kW) — out of scope.

drafts.title: Solid‑state high‑energy cells request (customer specification)
drafts.description: Customers request that the battery uses solid‑state cells with 400 Wh/kg energy density.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope (engineering/technology specification): requests for specific cell chemistry and energy density are engineering decisions; the customer outcome (higher real‑world range) is addressed in the long‑range requirement.
drafts.scope_reason: Engineering/technology specification (cell chemistry & Wh/kg) — out of scope for customer‑facing requirements.

drafts.title: Front brake disc diameter request (customer specification)
drafts.description: Customers request front brake discs with a diameter of 395 mm.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope (engineering specification): specific brake disc diameter is an engineering choice; the customer outcome (confident braking performance) should be addressed by braking performance requirements in the driving experience domain.
drafts.scope_reason: Engineering specification request (component dimension) — out of scope.

drafts.title: Request for a specific lidar supplier for highway assist
drafts.description: Customers ask that highway assist use a lidar sensor from a named supplier.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope (supplier/component specification): requests to use a named supplier are procurement/engineering matters; customer‑facing outcomes are covered by lane‑keeping and highway assist performance requirements.
drafts.scope_reason: Supplier/component selection request — out of scope for customer‑facing requirement drafting.
